target.text: Khoso ea permaculture bakeng sa lihoai tse nyane tsa Afrika Boroa.
Bala naha pele o e fetola. Fumana moo metsi a phallang teng, moo letsatsi le chabang teng, moo moea o fokang teng, le moo moea o batang o bokellanang teng.
Ditemoho tsena di tataisa dikgetho tse sebetsang bakeng sa dijalo, difate, meaho, ditsela le metsi. Ke qalo ya moralo o motle.
Ho Bala Ponahalo ea Naha
Polasi e ’ngoe le e ’ngoe e na le mekhoa e seng e sebetsa pele re eketsa letho.
Ha u bala mekhoa ena pele, u beha metsi, lijalo, lifate le meaho libakeng tseo li ka sebetsang le naha.
Hobaneng Taba Ena E Le Bohlokwa
Qetellong ea mojule ona, u tla khona ho latela metsi ho pholletsa le naha ea hao le ho fumana moo a tlohang teng.
U tla read sun angles, shade, wind, frost, and slope.
U tla sebelisa A-frame level ho latela contours.
U tla taka a simple site map with water flow, seasonal winds, frost pockets, existing vegetation, zones, and sectors.
Diphetho tsa ho Ithuta
Pele u kotula metsi, ithute moo a seng a ea teng.
Thuto ya 1: Moo Pula e Yang Teng
Shebella: Water Slows, Sinks, and Leaves
Trace Contours ka A-Frame
Sheba Metsi Pele U Haha
Sheba sebaka sa hao pele u khetha where to place tender crops, trees, or buildings.
Thuto 2: Bala Letsatsi le Moriti
Latela letsatsi, moaho, sefate, le meriti ea tsona ho pholletsa le letsoapo. Bapisa letsatsi le phahameng la lehlabula le letsatsi le tlase la mariha.
Shebella: Follow the Sun Across the Site
A wall or shade cloth can shade a bed longer in winter than in summer. Hlahloba shadows tsa sebele before you build or fix a shade structure in place.
Ema sebakeng seo at 8am, midday, and 4pm on a winter's day. Watch where the shade falls.
Hlahloba Winter Shadows pele o haha
Sireletsa frost-tender plants
Thuto 3: Read Wind, Frost, and Slope
Shebella: See Wind and Cold Air on the Map

Sheba ice and plant damage, compare low ground with slopes, and check minimum temperatures where you can. Mark places where cold or damage lasts longest. Keep sensitive plants away from the cold pockets you observe.
Khetha Airflow and Warmth
Ho etsa site map ho hloka paper, a tape measure, a compass, and time to walk your land.
Tsamaea moeling, ebe u etsa sketch ya pele. Mark it not to scale until you have checked its distances. Mark north. Add the house, trees, water, roads, and fences.
Joale taka the patterns you have observed. Your map becomes the design skeleton for the whole smallholding.
Thuto ya 4: Qala Mmapa wa hao wa Setsha
Sebelisa setšoantšo e le motataisi: moeli, meaho, litsela, metsi, matsoapo, le metsu ea tataiso. Thala se seng se ntse se le teng pele o rera liphetoho.
Shebella: Taka the Land You Already Have
Sheba libaka where frost sits longest and where the ground smells damp during dry months.
Ela hloko existing vegetation. Mark where khakibos or blackjack grows thick.
These plants can grow in disturbed places, but their presence alone does not show whether the soil is compacted. Hlahloba soil before deciding what the patch means for your design.
Lumella dimela di u thuse ho bala Soil
Tšoaea summer and winter wind ka thoko. They can come from different directions, so a windbreak or crop position that works in one season may be wrong in the other.
Beha your zones and sectors on the same base map.
Ntšhafatsa setshwantsho nako ya selemo le nako ya selemo. Mmapa wa pensele oo o hlileng o o sebedisang o bohlokwa ho feta mmapa o phethahetseng o thadilweng hanngwe feela.
Eketsa seasons, zones, le sectors
When it is safe after heavy rain, walk your land. Tšoaea rills, spreading water, ponds, and where water leaves your property. Note where excess water may need a safe route away.
Khutla ka dawn on a cold June morning. Mark mist, frozen dew, and the places frost lasts longest.
Pampiring, taka your boundary, mark north, and add the house, water, roads, fences, slopes, and existing vegetation.
Mosebetsi oa tšimong
